prompt_free_text:
This paper studies an interesting and timely problem: how to adapt concept bottleneck models built on top of foundation-model features when the deployment distribution shifts and only unlabeled target data are available. The paper’s central claim is that concept-based pipelines are not automatically robust under shift, even when they are interpretable and competitive in-domain, and that a dedicated test-time adaptation procedure can recover both accuracy and better-aligned concept explanations. The proposed method, CONDA, combines three components: concept-score alignment by adapting the concept bank, adaptation of the linear concept-to-label layer, and a residual concept bottleneck that adds new concepts online. The empirical section reports substantial gains across several datasets and several CBM construction methods.

Overall, I find the paper promising and potentially impactful. The problem is well motivated, especially because recent work has made CBMs practical on top of strong vision-language backbones, but deployment-time robustness of such interpretable pipelines has been underexplored. The paper also has a nice systems-level perspective: rather than treating interpretability and robustness as separate goals, it asks how to preserve concept-based decision making after deployment. The empirical gains on Waterbirds, Metashift, and Camelyon17 are substantial, and the qualitative discussion of how concept reliance changes under shift is compelling. That said, I also have several concerns about the technical framing, the strength of the theoretical claims, and some aspects of the experimental methodology that should be addressed before I would be fully convinced.

The strongest aspect of the paper is the problem formulation and empirical motivation. The observation that CBMs can match or exceed feature-based predictors on the source domain yet degrade sharply under shift is important and worth documenting. The distinction between adapting the concept extractor, the concept-to-label mapping, and the concept set itself is intuitive and useful. In particular, the residual concept bottleneck is a natural mechanism for handling incompleteness of the original concept bank, and this is arguably one of the most interesting contributions because it acknowledges a core limitation of CBMs in practice: the source concept vocabulary may simply be insufficient for the target domain.

I also appreciate that the method is source-free at adaptation time except for retained summary statistics and the source-trained models. This is a realistic setting. The use of multiple CBM construction methods and multiple backbones is another strength, since it suggests the approach is not tied to one specific concept discovery pipeline. The paper is also generally well written and easy to follow at a high level.

However, the paper’s formal treatment of distribution shift and completeness is not yet fully convincing. The definitions in Section 2 are mathematically dressed up, but they do not clearly yield actionable theoretical guarantees. For example, “low-level shift” is defined as one that leaves the concept-score distribution unchanged, and “concept-level shift” as one that changes concept scores but not prediction distributions. These are effectively definitional categories rather than properties that can be checked or inferred in practice. In fact, the main empirical point of the paper is that under corruptions commonly thought of as low-level, the concept-score distribution often does change for the deployed CBM. So the formalism risks becoming circular: a shift is “low-level” if concept scores should not change, but when they do change, the model is declared non-robust. This is not wrong, but it weakens the explanatory value of the taxonomy.

Similarly, the completeness definition is quite strong and somewhat underspecified. It says a concept set is complete if there exists a classifier over concepts whose prediction distribution is invariant across source and target under both low-level and concept-level shifts. But this notion depends on the hypothesis class, the target shift family, and only matches distributions of predictions rather than correctness or Bayes optimality. It is also not clear how this relates to existing notions of sufficiency/completeness in the CBM literature. As written, the formal section reads more like conceptual scaffolding than theory. That is acceptable if presented modestly, but the paper currently leans a bit too heavily on “formal categorization” language without deriving guarantees, impossibility results, or even testable implications.

On the method side, the three-stage design is sensible, but some choices feel heuristic and need stronger justification. The CSA objective assumes class-conditional Gaussianity of concept scores and requires access to source-domain class means and covariances. This is a nontrivial retained artifact from source training, and the paper should be clearer about whether storing these statistics is always allowed under the claimed source-free setting. More importantly, the Gaussian assumption may be poor for concept scores, especially for sparse or highly correlated concept banks. The Mahalanobis-based ratio loss is borrowed from prior feature alignment work, but why it is especially appropriate in concept space is not deeply argued. Since concept scores are often semantically heterogeneous and may have very different marginal behaviors, some empirical validation of the Gaussian approximation would help.

The pseudo-labeling strategy is another important source of concern. The method relies on an ensemble of zero-shot and linear-probe predictions from the FM, selecting the more confident one. This is a strong auxiliary signal, and in some sense the adaptation quality may depend more on the robustness of these non-interpretable predictors than on the CBM adaptation mechanism itself. The paper acknowledges this, but the implications are significant. If the pseudo-labeler is already very strong, then CONDA may be functioning partly as a distillation or projection of a robust black-box predictor into a concept-based parameterization. That is still useful, but it changes the interpretation of the contribution. I would like to see a clearer disentangling of how much gain comes from the pseudo-label source versus the adaptation objectives. For example, how does performance change if pseudo-labels come only from the source CBM, only from zero-shot, only from linear probing, or from confidence-thresholded subsets? The appendix may contain some of this, but the main paper should make the dependence more transparent.

There is also a conceptual tension between interpretability and the residual branch. The residual concept bottleneck adds randomly initialized concept vectors and optimizes them directly for target accuracy with regularizers for diversity and coherence. This may improve performance, but whether these learned vectors correspond to stable, human-meaningful concepts is less clear. The paper presents a few automatically annotated examples such as feathers, wings, and beak, which is encouraging, but this is not enough to establish that the residual branch generally preserves CBM-style interpretability rather than introducing latent directions that are only post hoc named. Since interpretability is a central claim, the paper should evaluate it more systematically. For instance, one could measure concept coherence, concept sparsity, overlap with known attributes where available, or human agreement on concept labels before and after adaptation. Without such evidence, the claim that CONDA yields “concept-based interpretations better aligned with the test data” remains suggestive rather than firmly demonstrated.

The experimental results are mixed in a way that deserves more careful discussion. On Waterbirds and Metashift, the gains are indeed impressive, especially in worst-group accuracy. On Camelyon17, gains are also meaningful. But on CIFAR100, the strongest CBM baseline from Yeh et al. actually degrades after adaptation in both AVG and WG, and several other settings show negligible or negative WG changes. Even on CIFAR10, one CBM baseline degrades after adaptation. This does not invalidate the method, but it weakens the broad claim that CONDA “aligns the CBM performance with that of non-interpretable classification.” In several cases, adapted CBMs remain well below LP or even below the best unadapted CBM. The paper should present a more nuanced summary, perhaps emphasizing that CONDA is especially effective under concept-level and natural shifts, while under some low-level shifts or with already strong concept banks, adaptation can hurt.

Relatedly, the ablation narrative says CSA is most useful for low-level shifts and LPA/RCB for concept-level shifts, but the main quantitative evidence shown is only relative gains for one CBM family. Given the heterogeneity across CBM construction methods in Table 1, I would want to know whether this decomposition is robust across methods and datasets. It would also be useful to compare against simpler baselines: adapting only the linear probe on FM features and then projecting explanations post hoc; adapting only the CBM linear layer with standard entropy minimization; or applying existing TTA methods directly to the FM classifier and then comparing accuracy/interpretability tradeoffs. The paper compares to ZS and LP as non-adapted baselines, but not to adapted non-interpretable baselines. Since the claim is partly that CONDA recovers performance “on par with” non-interpretable classification under shift, the relevant comparison should include strong TTA baselines on the FM pipeline, not just static ZS/LP.

Another issue is evaluation protocol. The method uses online adaptation over sequential batches of the test set, and predictions are made after adapting on the same batch. This follows common TTA practice, but it can make results sensitive to batch order, batch size, and class composition. The paper mentions random batching, but I would like clearer reporting of sensitivity to these choices. In particular, for group robustness metrics like WG, batch composition could matter a lot. Also, because pseudo-labels are generated from the same batch being adapted on, there is a risk of confirmation bias. Confidence filtering or calibration analysis would strengthen the case.

There are a few technical details that need clarification or correction. The Mahalanobis distance formula in the text appears to have a parenthesis typo. The notation around Eq. 5 and references to Eq. 3/4 in later sections is somewhat inconsistent. The coherence regularizer is maximized via a negative sign in the loss, but its interpretation could be explained more carefully. The cosine similarity regularizer in Eq. 12 seems to penalize raw cosine similarity rather than absolute similarity; if negative cosine values are allowed, minimizing this term could encourage anti-alignment rather than orthogonality, which may or may not be intended. Also, because concept vectors are normalized in some places but not obviously constrained during optimization in others, it would help to specify whether re-normalization is performed after each gradient step.

I also think the paper should discuss more explicitly the privacy/storage implications of retaining source statistics and the source linear probe. In some source-free adaptation settings, retaining class-conditional covariance matrices may be acceptable, but in others it may not. Since the paper emphasizes no access to source data, it should be precise about what source-derived artifacts are assumed available.

In terms of novelty, the paper is solid but somewhat incremental methodologically. CSA is adapted from class-aware feature alignment ideas, LPA is essentially pseudo-label fine-tuning of the linear layer with sparsity regularization, and RCB resembles residual concept expansion ideas from recent CBM work. The novelty lies more in the integration of these pieces for FM-based CBMs under source-free TTA, plus the empirical demonstration that different components matter under different shift types. I think that is enough for a worthwhile contribution if the empirical evidence is strong and the claims are calibrated, but it is not a paper with deep new theory or a fundamentally new adaptation principle.

My main suggestions for improvement are as follows. First, strengthen the empirical comparisons by including adapted non-interpretable baselines and simpler CBM adaptation baselines. Second, provide a more systematic analysis of pseudo-label quality and its effect on performance. Third, evaluate interpretability more rigorously, especially for residual concepts, rather than relying mainly on anecdotal examples. Fourth, tone down or sharpen the formal section: either derive concrete propositions from the taxonomy or present it more explicitly as an organizing framework rather than a theoretical contribution. Fifth, discuss failure cases more openly, especially the settings where adaptation hurts. Finally, clarify implementation details around normalization, covariance estimation, batch sensitivity, and source-retained statistics.

In summary, I view this as a good paper on an important problem, with strong motivation and promising empirical results, especially under concept-level shifts. Its main weakness is that some of the theoretical framing overstates what is actually established, and some of the empirical claims about interpretability and broad robustness need stronger support. If revised to better calibrate claims and strengthen the experimental analysis, this could be a valuable contribution to the literature on interpretable adaptation for foundation-model pipelines.

My recommendation is borderline positive. I would lean toward acceptance if the venue values timely empirical contributions at the intersection of interpretability and robustness, but I would want the authors to address the concerns above, especially around baselines, pseudo-label dependence, and interpretability evaluation.

prompt_structured_json.summary: The paper studies test-time adaptation for concept bottleneck models (CBMs) built on top of foundation model features under distribution shift. It identifies three failure modes for deployed CBMs: non-robust concept mappings under low-level shifts, non-robust concept-to-label classifiers under concept-level shifts, and incomplete concept sets. To address these, it proposes CONDA, a three-stage source-free adaptation pipeline using only unlabeled target data: (1) Concept Score Alignment (CSA), which adapts concept vectors by minimizing a class-aware Mahalanobis alignment loss using source-domain concept statistics and pseudo-labels; (2) Linear Probing Adaptation (LPA), which adapts the concept-to-label linear layer with pseudo-labeled cross-entropy and elastic-net regularization; and (3) Residual Concept Bottleneck (RCB), which adds new residual concepts and a residual classifier trained with pseudo-labeled cross-entropy plus similarity/coherency regularization. Experiments on CIFAR10/100-C, Waterbirds, Metashift, and Camelyon17 with several CBM construction methods show substantial gains over unadapted CBMs, often bringing performance closer to non-interpretable zero-shot or linear-probe baselines. The paper also presents qualitative evidence that adapted concepts better reflect target-domain correlations.
strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored problem: test-time/source-free adaptation for interpretable concept bottleneck pipelines built on foundation models.
The decomposition into three failure modes is intuitive and helps motivate the modular design of CSA, LPA, and RCB.
Method is practically appealing in the source-free unlabeled target setting and does not require updating the foundation model backbone.
Empirical evaluation spans multiple datasets, multiple shift types, and multiple CBM construction methods, which strengthens the practical relevance of the findings.
Results show large improvements over unadapted CBMs on several benchmarks, especially under concept-level shifts such as Waterbirds and Metashift.
The qualitative interpretability analysis is a useful addition and suggests that residual concepts can capture missing target-domain semantics.
The method is modular, and the component-wise ablation narrative is sensible: CSA helps more for low-level shifts, while LPA/RCB help more for concept-level shifts.
weaknesses: The theoretical framing of shift types and completeness is largely definitional and does not yield formal guarantees, identifiable conditions, or testable consequences; several claims are therefore more motivational than rigorous.

The method relies heavily on pseudo-label quality from zero-shot/linear-probe FM predictors, but the paper does not fully isolate how much of the gains come from strong pseudo-labels versus the proposed adaptation machinery.

CSA assumes access to source-domain class-conditional Gaussian statistics of concept scores, which is a nontrivial form of source information and weakens the practical purity of the claimed source-free setting.

The empirical comparison is mostly against unadapted CBMs and non-interpretable baselines, with limited direct comparison to strong generic test-time adaptation baselines applied to the same CBM or linear-head setting.

Some results are inconsistent with the broad claim that CONDA improves performance: on CIFAR100 and Camelyon17 with the Yeh et al. CBM, adaptation degrades target AVG/WG, and on some settings worst-group accuracy also drops.

Interpretability claims are suggestive but not rigorously quantified; better alignment of concepts to target data is mostly supported by qualitative examples rather than systematic human or automatic evaluation.
The method introduces many stages and hyperparameters, increasing complexity and making it harder to attribute gains cleanly or assess robustness of tuning in realistic deployment.
methodological_flaws: The scientific logic in Section 2 is somewhat circular: low-level shift is defined as one that does not change the concept-score distribution, yet a key failure mode is that the concept bottleneck is not robust under low-level shift because the concept-score distribution changes. This makes the taxonomy partly dependent on the chosen concept mapping rather than the underlying data shift, weakening the conceptual clarity of the formalization.

Definition 1 of concept completeness is weak and nonstandard: equality of prediction distributions across domains does not imply correct labels or sufficiency of concepts for classification. A classifier could match prediction distributions while being wrong instance-wise. Thus the definition does not formally capture semantic completeness or sufficiency in the usual CBM sense.

The CSA objective is only a heuristic surrogate for class-conditional distribution alignment. Minimizing log(D_intra/D_inter) for pseudo-labeled samples does not in general imply alignment of target class-conditional distributions to source Gaussians, especially under class-prior shift, multimodal concept distributions, or pseudo-label noise.

The Gaussian assumption for class-conditional concept scores is unvalidated and potentially poor for high-dimensional concept spaces. The method depends on covariance inversion, but the paper does not discuss regularization, conditioning, or stability when m is large or class sample sizes are limited.

The pseudo-labeling protocol may leak substantial predictive power from non-interpretable models into the adapted CBM. Since pseudo-labels are chosen from an ensemble of zero-shot and linear-probe predictors and then used to train/adapt the CBM, improvements may largely reflect distillation from these stronger predictors rather than intrinsic adaptation of concepts. This weakens claims that the method itself closes the gap to non-interpretable models.

The evaluation does not convincingly establish fairness against alternative adaptation strategies. For example, adapting only the linear probe on FM features, or applying standard TTA methods directly to the CBM logits/features, would be important baselines to determine whether concept-specific adaptation is necessary.

The online adaptation protocol can be order-sensitive, but the paper does not analyze sensitivity to batch order, batch size, or streaming nonstationarity. This is important because online TTA methods can vary substantially with data ordering.

The residual branch is claimed to improve interpretability, but residual concepts are randomly initialized and optimized only through pseudo-labeled classification plus heuristic regularizers. Without stronger constraints or human validation, there is limited evidence that these learned directions correspond to stable, human-meaningful concepts rather than generic discriminative features.

There appears to be at least one notation/reference inconsistency: Section 3.2 refers to predictions of the target-domain CBM via Eqn. (3), but the target-domain CBM is defined later as Eqn. (5). Such inconsistencies do not invalidate the method but reduce confidence in mathematical presentation rigor.

Empirically, some adapted variants underperform the unadapted CBM, yet the paper's headline framing emphasizes broad gains. A more careful statistical analysis and discussion of failure cases is needed to support claims of robustness and reliability.
